stem: Which is the correct heading for a column of gas volumes in a results table?

options.rationale: Quantity, then a solidus, then the unit.
The quantity comes first, then the unit.
The unit is missing, so every value would need its own unit.
This is a different quantity (a rate) with no unit.

explanation: Column headings give the physical quantity and its unit, for example 'volume of gas / cm³'. The values in the column are then written as numbers only.

stem: A student repeats a timing four times and records 42 s, 41 s, 55 s and 43 s. Which result is anomalous?

options.rationale: It is far from the other three, which agree within 2 s.
41 s agrees well with 42 s and 43 s.
42 s fits the pattern.
55 s clearly does not fit.

explanation: The other times agree within 2 s, but 55 s is more than 10 s away from them. It is anomalous and should be left out of the mean (and repeated if possible).

stem: Four repeat measurements of a temperature rise are 7.2 °C, 7.4 °C, 5.1 °C and 7.3 °C. The value 5.1 °C is anomalous. Calculate the mean of the other three results.
hints: Do not include the anomalous value.

stem: True or false: the independent variable is usually plotted on the x-axis of a graph.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: the variable you change goes on the x-axis and the one you measure on the y-axis.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: the independent variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis.

explanation: By convention the independent variable (what you change) is on the x-axis and the dependent variable (what you measure) is on the y-axis.

stem: How should a line be drawn through experimental points on a graph?

options.content: by joining each point to the next one with a ruler
options.rationale: Dot-to-dot lines follow every random error.

options.content: through the first and last points only, with a ruler
options.rationale: The middle points matter just as much.

options.content: always through the origin, whatever the data show
options.rationale: Only draw through the origin if the data and the science justify it.

options.content: as one smooth line or curve of best fit, ignoring anomalies
options.rationale: This shows the overall trend.

explanation: A line of best fit is one straight line or smooth curve with the points scattered evenly about it. Anomalous points are ignored.

stem: A graph of mass of product (in g) against time (in minutes) is a straight line passing through (0, 0) and (5.0, 3.0). Calculate the gradient of the line, in g/min.
explanation: Gradient $= \dfrac{\text{change in mass}}{\text{change in time}} = \dfrac{3.0 - 0}{5.0 - 0} = 0.60$ g/min.
workedSolution:
1. Change in $y = 3.0$ g; change in $x = 5.0$ min.
2. Gradient $= 3.0 \div 5.0 = 0.60$ g/min.
hints: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.

stem:
The volume of gas collected in 30 s was measured at different acid concentrations. The points lie on a straight line through the origin.

| concentration / mol/dm³ | 0.50 | 1.00 | 1.50 | 2.00 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| volume in 30 s / cm³ | 12 | 24 | 36 | 48 |

Use interpolation to estimate the volume collected in 30 s at 1.25 mol/dm³.
explanation: The volume rises by 12 cm³ for every 0.50 mol/dm³ (24 cm³ per 1 mol/dm³). At 1.25 mol/dm³: $1.25 \times 24 = 30$ cm³, halfway between 24 and 36 cm³.

stem: Results were collected for acid concentrations from 0.5 to 2.0 mol/dm³. A student extends the line to estimate the result at 3.0 mol/dm³. What is this called?

options.rationale: Interpolation reads between the plotted points.
An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern.
A gradient is the steepness of the line.
Extending the line beyond the measured range.

explanation: Extrapolation estimates a value outside the range of the measurements by extending the line. It is less reliable than interpolation because the trend may change.

stem:
Marble chips react with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The volume of carbon dioxide is recorded.

| time / s | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120 | 150 | 180 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| volume of gas / cm³ | 0 | 40 | 65 | 80 | 88 | 90 | 90 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the total volume of gas produced.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: In which time interval did the reaction stop?

options.rationale: The volume still increases from 88 to 90 cm³ after 120 s.
The volume is already 90 cm³ at 150 s.
There is no further gas after 150 s.
The volume reaches 90 cm³ by 150 s and then stays constant.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean rate of reaction over the first 60 s, in cm³/s, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: In which interval was the rate greatest?

options.rationale: 40 cm³ was produced: the most in any 30 s interval.
Only 25 cm³ was produced.
Only 15 cm³ was produced.
No gas was produced.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the rate decreases as the reaction proceeds.

points.description: The reactants (acid and/or marble) are used up, so their concentration/amount decreases
So there are fewer collisions per second between acid particles and the marble surface

parts.explanation: As the reaction goes on, acid particles and marble are used up, so the concentration of acid falls. There are fewer collisions per second between acid particles and the marble surface, so the rate decreases until the limiting reactant is used up.

explanation: The curve levels off at 90 cm³ between 120 and 150 s. The mean rate in the first 60 s is 65 ÷ 60 = 1.08 cm³/s. The fastest interval is the first, because the concentration of acid is highest at the start.
hints: Look for where the volume stops changing.

stem: A graph of volume of gas against time is a curve. How do you find the rate of reaction at exactly 60 s? (Cambridge Extended)

options.content: Divide the volume at 60 s by 60.
options.rationale: This gives the mean rate from 0 to 60 s, not the rate at 60 s.

options.content: Read the volume of gas at 60 s.
options.rationale: A volume is not a rate.

options.content: Draw a tangent to the curve at 60 s and calculate its gradient.
options.rationale: The gradient of the tangent is the rate at that instant.

options.content: Find the gradient of a line joining the first and last points.
options.rationale: This gives the mean rate for the whole reaction.

explanation:
The rate at an instant is the gradient of the curve at that point. Draw a tangent touching the curve at 60 s and calculate its gradient (change in volume ÷ change in time).

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Which line has the same steepness as the curve at 60 s?

stem: A tangent is drawn to a volume–time curve at t = 40 s. The tangent passes through the points (0 s, 14 cm³) and (80 s, 78 cm³). Calculate the rate of reaction at 40 s in cm³/s. (Cambridge Extended)
explanation:
Gradient of the tangent $= \dfrac{78 - 14}{80 - 0} = \dfrac{64}{80} = 0.80$ cm³/s.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
workedSolution:
1. Change in volume $= 78 - 14 = 64$ cm³.
2. Change in time $= 80 - 0 = 80$ s.
3. Rate $= 64 \div 80 = 0.80$ cm³/s.
hints: Use the two points on the tangent, not on the curve.

stem: Zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution in a glass beaker. The temperature rises from 21.6 °C to a maximum of 27.4 °C.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The temperature rise is smaller than the rise calculated from the data-book enthalpy change. Which is the most likely main source of error?

options.content: The thermometer read about 1 °C too high.
options.rationale: A thermometer reading too high would not make the rise smaller.

options.content: Too much zinc powder was added to the solution.
options.rationale: Excess zinc makes sure all the copper ions react.

options.content: Heat was lost from the solution through the glass beaker.
options.rationale: Glass conducts heat away and the top was open.

options.content: The solution was stirred during the reaction.
options.rationale: Stirring helps reach a true maximum temperature.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest two improvements to the experiment.

points.description: Use an insulated container (polystyrene cup) with a lid to reduce heat loss
Stir continuously and record the highest temperature / use a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C / repeat and take a mean

parts.explanation: Carry out the reaction in a polystyrene cup with a lid to cut heat loss, stir continuously and record the highest temperature reached, use a thermometer that reads to 0.1 °C, and repeat the experiment to calculate a mean temperature rise.

explanation: The rise is 27.4 − 21.6 = 5.8 °C. Heat lost through the glass and the open top makes the measured rise too small; insulation, a lid, stirring, a more precise thermometer and repeats improve the result.
hints: Where could the heat released by the reaction go?

stem: Complete the rules for results tables.

payload.template: Units are written in the column {{blank:where}}, and all the values in a column should have the same number of {{blank:what}}.

explanation: Units go in the column heading (quantity / unit), and values in a column are recorded to the same number of decimal places, matching the instrument.

stem: The volumes of gas to be plotted range from 0 to 37 cm³. The y-axis is 10 large squares long. Which scale is best?

options.rationale: The data would use less than half of the axis.
37 cm³ would need more than 12 squares, so the data would not fit on the axis; multiples of 3 are also awkward to plot and read.
37 cm³ then fills more than seven squares, and 5 is an easy step to plot.
Multiples of 8 are awkward, and the data would fill under half of the axis.

explanation: A good scale uses more than half of the grid and goes up in steps of 1, 2, 5 or 10. With 5 cm³ per square, 37 cm³ reaches 7.4 squares.
hints: Check how much of the axis the data would use for each choice.

stem: True or false: repeat results that agree very closely with each other can still be inaccurate.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: for example, a thermometer that always reads 2 °C too high gives results that agree with each other but are all wrong by the same amount.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Close agreement shows the results are repeatable, but an instrument error can make them all wrong by the same amount.

explanation: Repeatability (close agreement) is not the same as accuracy (closeness to the true value). An error that affects every reading in the same way, such as a balance that is not zeroed, shifts all the results without making them disagree.
hints: Think of an instrument that is wrong by the same amount every time.

stem: Match each term with its meaning.

right.content: a result that does not fit the pattern of the others
reading a value from a graph between the plotted points
extending a line beyond the plotted points to estimate a value
the sum of the values divided by the number of values
the steepness of a line on a graph

explanation: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern; interpolation reads between points; extrapolation goes beyond them; the mean is the average. The steepness of a line is its gradient.

stem: In a reaction, 24 cm³ of gas is collected in the first 2 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of reaction in cm³ per second.
explanation: 2 minutes $= 120$ s. Mean rate $= 24 \div 120 = 0.20$ cm³/s.

stem:
Nyasha times how long marble chips of the same mass and size take to dissolve completely in hydrochloric acid of different concentrations at the same temperature.

| concentration of acid / mol/dm³ | 0.50 | 1.00 | 1.50 | 2.00 | 2.50 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| time / s | 240 | 118 | 82 | 75 | 48 |

options.rationale: This fits: doubling to 1.00 mol/dm³ roughly halves the time.
The pattern (time roughly halves when concentration doubles) predicts about 60 s.
This fits the pattern (about 240 ÷ 3 = 80 s).
This fits (about 240 ÷ 5 = 48 s).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest a possible cause of the anomalous result.

points.description: A specific plausible cause, e.g. the acid was diluted wrongly / the chip was larger / the acid was colder / the timer was stopped late

parts.explanation: The 2.00 mol/dm³ acid may have been made up wrongly (too dilute), the marble chip may have been slightly larger, the acid may have been colder, or the stop-watch may have been stopped late.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The rate can be represented by 1 ÷ time. Calculate 1 ÷ time for the 0.50 mol/dm³ experiment, in s⁻¹, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which conclusion do the reliable results support?

options.content: The time taken is directly proportional to the concentration.
options.rationale: The time falls as the concentration rises.

options.content: Doubling concentration about halves the time: rate ∝ concentration.
Concentration has no clear effect on the rate of reaction.
options.rationale: The times change a lot.

options.content: The rate decreases as the acid concentration increases.
options.rationale: Shorter times mean faster rates.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest one improvement to make the results more reliable.

points.description: Repeat each concentration (at least twice) and calculate a mean / control the temperature with a water bath / measure gas volume instead of judging disappearance

parts.explanation: Repeat each concentration two or three times and calculate the mean time, so anomalous results can be identified, and keep the temperature constant with a water bath.

explanation: The times fall roughly in inverse proportion to concentration (240, 120, 80, 60, 48 s expected), so 75 s at 2.00 mol/dm³ is anomalous. 1 ÷ 240 = 0.00417 s⁻¹. Doubling the concentration halves the time, so the rate is about proportional to concentration.
workedSolution:
1. (a) Expected time at 2.00 mol/dm³ $\approx 240 \div 4 = 60$ s; 75 s does not fit.
2. (c) $1 \div 240 = 0.004167 \approx 0.00417\ \text{s}^{-1}$.
hints: Compare each time with 240 s divided by (concentration ÷ 0.50).

stem: In a series of timing experiments, a student always starts the stop-watch about 3 seconds after adding the acid. What effect does this have on the recorded times?

options.content: All the recorded times are about 3 s too long.
options.rationale: Starting late misses time, so the times are shorter.

options.content: All the recorded times are about 3 s too short.
options.rationale: The first 3 s of each reaction are never timed.

options.content: The times are randomly too long or too short.
options.rationale: The error is the same each time, in the same direction.

options.content: There is no effect because the error is the same every time.
options.rationale: It still makes every time wrong, even if comparisons are less affected.

explanation: Starting the stop-watch late misses the first few seconds of every run, so every recorded time is too short by about the same amount. This kind of error affects all results in the same direction.
hints: Which part of each reaction is not timed?

stem: What name is given to a result that does not fit the pattern of the other results?
explanation: A result that does not fit the pattern is an anomalous result (an anomaly). It is left out of means and lines of best fit, and its cause is investigated.
